non-absolutist objectivism: "Moral objectivism is right + there are objective values (e.g. protect the innocent, honesty, loyalty, pleasure - utilitarianism), but they cannot be captured in rules that apply in all cases without regard for circumstances" (slide 5); it can say "it depends", on "the relevant circumstances of the action", which is not relativism (slide 6). See [Rejecting relativism leaves open which theory tells you what to do](#/libs7102-l4/from-relativism-to-theories).
white hat hacking|white hat: "White hat hacking - with permission (paid and legal penetration tester)" (slide 8). See [White, black and grey hats differ by permission and intent; utilitarianism looks only at outcomes](#/libs7102-l4/hats-of-hacking).
black hat hacking|black hat: "Black hat hacking - without permission. Goal is to steal data, destroy data, make the network unusable, steal confidential info, etc" (slide 8). See [White, black and grey hats differ by permission and intent; utilitarianism looks only at outcomes](#/libs7102-l4/hats-of-hacking).
grey hat hacking|grey hat: "Grey hat hackers can break the law, but then not take advantage, or even offer to fix security issue" (slide 8); common sense says "Possibly – But how can we tell?". See [White, black and grey hats differ by permission and intent; utilitarianism looks only at outcomes](#/libs7102-l4/hats-of-hacking).
consequentialism|consequentialist theory: "Because utilitarianism determines morality based on consequences, we call it a consequentialist theory of normative ethics"; "Actions are good if their consequences are useful" (slide 12). See [Bentham: pleasure and pain are our two sovereign masters, and utility is the test of right](#/libs7102-l4/bentham-and-the-principle-of-utility).
psychological hedonism|motivational hedo: "Pleasure and pain are the ultimate explanations for action" (slide 13): a descriptive claim about what we shall do. See [Bentham: pleasure and pain are our two sovereign masters, and utility is the test of right](#/libs7102-l4/bentham-and-the-principle-of-utility).
normative hedonism: "Pleasure is the only intrinsic good, pain the only intrinsic bad. The tradition comes from Epicurus (Ancient Greece)" (slide 13): a claim about what we ought to do. See [Bentham: pleasure and pain are our two sovereign masters, and utility is the test of right](#/libs7102-l4/bentham-and-the-principle-of-utility).
principle of utility: Bentham: the principle "which approves or disapproves of every action whatsoever, according to the tendency which it appears to have to augment or diminish the happiness of the party whose interest is in question"; correctly read, "what we should actually do is what increases happiness/decreases pain the most of all available options" (slide 14). See [Bentham: pleasure and pain are our two sovereign masters, and utility is the test of right](#/libs7102-l4/bentham-and-the-principle-of-utility).
equal consideration of interests|ECI: "The pleasure or pain of one person should be of no more value than the pleasure or pain of another"; "Not a principal of equal treatment or just distribution" (slide 15); "ECI does NOT mean individuals are always treated equally" and "Utilitarianism is not about serving the interests of the 'majority'" (slide 16). See [Equal consideration counts everyone's interests equally; it does not treat everyone equally](#/libs7102-l4/equal-consideration-of-interests).
view from the universe: "Take a perfectly impartial 'view from the universe' – Sidgwick" (slide 15): the standpoint from which every affected interest counts equally. See [Equal consideration counts everyone's interests equally; it does not treat everyone equally](#/libs7102-l4/equal-consideration-of-interests).
felicific calculus|hedonic calculus: Bentham's measure of pleasure and pain by intensity, duration, certainty, proximity, fecundity, purity and extent ("the number of people affected by the action"); "pre-Mill utilitarianism and was not kept by Mill" (slide 18). See [Bentham measures pleasure on seven dimensions, so no kind of action is wrong in itself](#/libs7102-l4/felicific-calculus-and-no-intrinsic-wrong).
rejection of absolutism (Bentham): "No type of action (e.g. stealing, lying) is intrinsically right or wrong. This is a rejection of absolutism. Actions can only be wrong when they fail to be appropriate means to maximizing utility" (slide 18). See [Bentham measures pleasure on seven dimensions, so no kind of action is wrong in itself](#/libs7102-l4/felicific-calculus-and-no-intrinsic-wrong).
Greatest Happiness Principle|GHP: Mill's principle that *actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness*; correctly read, *an action is right if and only if there is no other available action the agent could have done instead that has higher utility* (slide 24). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
utility|net utility: *Utility = net of Pleasure - Pain*; we *maximize utility*, not pleasure, *as the available action with most utility may involve pain* (slide 24). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
quality of pleasure|higher pleasures: Mill's addition to Bentham: *there are also differences of quality in utility*; *better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied* (slide 22). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
competent judges: Those *who have experience of both* pleasures; the one *all or almost all* of them prefer, *irrespective of any feeling of moral obligation*, is the more desirable (slide 25). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
internal sanctions: Mill's emotional sources of moral motivation, *self-esteem, guilt, and conscience*, *formed by education and social environment*; the basis of his rejection of Bentham's psychological egoism (slide 22). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
Mill's proof|proof of the principle of u: *The sole evidence it is possible to produce that anything is desirable is that people do actually desire it*, by analogy with visible and seen; Bentham had said the principle *does not admit of direct proof* (slide 26). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
concrete action|generic action: *Concrete (Paul steals an apple) vs. generic action (stealing)*; the utility principle is about *the normative status of concrete actions only* (slide 27). See [Mill adds quality to pleasure, and the right action is the one no alternative beats](#/libs7102-l4/mill-refines-bentham).
utilitarian algorithm: *1) identify all affected by available options for action 2) for each available action, aggregate all relevant utility ... using ECI ... considering the actual outcome and 3) choose the option that maximizes utility* (Lecture 5 slide 8). See [Right means maximizing actual utility, a test of actions, not a decision procedure](#/libs7102-l4/the-utilitarian-algorithm).
criterion of right|decision procedure: The principle of utility *is not a decision procedure. It is merely a criterion of right*; *utilitarianism doesn't demand or expect that a utilitarian must calculate utility at all before acting* (week 4 notes). See [Right means maximizing actual utility, a test of actions, not a decision procedure](#/libs7102-l4/the-utilitarian-algorithm).
no ought without can: *If an action is not available (it is simply impossible to do it), then there is no moral obligation to perform it*, shared by all moral theories (week 4 notes). See [Right means maximizing actual utility, a test of actions, not a decision procedure](#/libs7102-l4/the-utilitarian-algorithm).
Jim and the twenty|kill one to save nine: Bernard Williams's case: Jim may kill one of twenty prisoners and the rest go free, or refuse and *Pedro will ... kill them all* (slide 29); utilitarianism says kill one. See [Jim and the twenty: utilitarianism says kill one to save nineteen](#/libs7102-l4/jim-and-the-twenty).
fat man variant|trolley problem: The trolley heading for five can be switched onto one (slide 31), or stopped only by pushing a man off a footbridge (*Fat man variant (Philippa Foot)*, slide 32); for utilitarianism both are *not just advised - they are morally required* (slide 34). See [The trolley, the fat man, Strangelove and Andy: utilitarianism makes the outcome decide](#/libs7102-l4/trolley-fat-man-strangelove-andy).
